passage:
At his new school in Johannesburg, Siddiq began copying how the football crowd talked, dropping his mother's language on the phone, wearing the same low-slung jeans and laughing at jokes he didn't get. On Friday he skipped chess club, because it wasn't cool.
Thabo caught up with him at the gate. "You're doing an impression of somebody."
Siddiq shrugged, then admitted it. "I just want them to like me."
"Fine. Wear the jeans, learn the slang. But I liked you when you were explaining the Sicilian defence."
That weekend Siddiq still hung out with the football group, but he brought a chess board along, and wore what he wanted. Two boys asked to play.

qa.q: Which club did Siddiq skip on Friday?
How did Siddiq feel at his new school, and what did he do about it?
qa.a: He felt insecure and anxious to be liked, admitting "I just want them to like me", so he copied the football crowd's talk and clothes.

qa.q: How did Siddiq balance fitting in with staying himself?
qa.a: He kept some of the group's style but brought his chess board and wore what he wanted, so he adapted lightly and kept his core.

qa.q: How does Thabo see Siddiq's change?
qa.a: Thabo sees a friend doing an impression of somebody else, and reminds him that he was liked for who he was, chess included.

grounding: Shows a teen changing his talk and dress to fit in, and Thabo helping him keep his core.

Tanvir: why do your voice notes sound like a different person now 😅
Kavitha: what do you mean
Tanvir: 'like, literally, no cap'?? you used to say 'enna da' every two lines
Kavitha: everyone here talks like that. if I talk like home they do this little smirk
Tanvir: and the pink rain boots? you loved those
Kavitha: under my bed. they only wear white sneakers here
Tanvir: ok but do you actually like the sneakers
Kavitha: ...they hurt my heels tbh
Tanvir: lol. you can pick up their slang, that's normal. but you're the funniest person I know when you're being you
Kavitha: I miss being me a bit 😔
Kavitha: fine. rain boots tomorrow. and I'm keeping 'enna da'
Tanvir: if they don't like it, they're not your people yet
Kavitha: Ishita laughed at my 'enna da' today actually. the nice kind of laugh

qa.q: Where are Kavitha's pink rain boots now?
What was Kavitha feeling when typing 'I miss being me a bit'?
qa.a: Kavitha felt sad and a little lost, homesick for the old way of talking and dressing 😔

qa.q: What would you advise Kavitha about fitting in?
qa.a: Pick up some slang if it's fun, but keep the rain boots and 'enna da'; people who need Kavitha hidden aren't close friends yet.

qa.q: How does Tanvir see the new way Kavitha talks?
qa.a: Tanvir finds it strange and a bit sad, missing the funny friend who talked like home.

grounding: Shows a teen changing speech and clothes to fit in, then choosing to adapt lightly while keeping habits that feel like home.

passage: In the first week of the college bus from Wadgaon to the taluka town, Madhuri stopped speaking her village Marathi. The town girls laughed at words like 'lai bhari', so she copied their neat, careful sentences and kept her bajra bhakri wrapped in her bag until she got home, hungry. By the third week her jaw ached from smiling at jokes she didn't find funny. One afternoon Avni from the back seat pulled out her own tiffin. 'My Aaji's thecha. Too spicy for these town people,' she grinned, in full village Marathi. Madhuri laughed before she could stop herself. 'Lai bhari,' she said, and unwrapped her bhakri. They shared it all the way home. Madhuri still used some town words in class; they were useful there. But on the bus she talked like herself, and the girls who smirked mattered a little less every day.

qa.q: What did Madhuri keep wrapped in her bag?
qa.a: Her bajra bhakri, until she got home, hungry.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling as her jaw ached from smiling?
qa.a: She felt tired and hollow, pretending to enjoy jokes just to belong.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Madhuri, and why?
qa.a: Keeping some town words for class but talking like herself on the bus, so she fits in lightly without hiding who she is.

qa.q: How does Avni see village Marathi on the bus?
qa.a: Avni is proud of it and jokes about town people, which makes it safe for Madhuri to be herself too.

grounding: Shows a teen who hides her dialect and food to fit in, then adapts lightly while keeping her core with a friend who accepts it.
